result.markdown: --- title: "Session 4 — Interaction and Effect Modification" subtitle: "Product terms · simple slopes · centring · emtrends · categorical interactions · additive scale · testing · Lab 4" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Sessions 1 to 3: the **shape** of one predictor's effect - Today: when the **effect of one variable depends on another** (**effect modification**) - By the end you can: - fit and read a **product term** - compute **simple slopes** with `emtrends` - **centre** a variable to interpret main effects - interpret an interaction on the **additive and multiplicative scale** - avoid the **subgroup p-value trap** ::: # Topic 1 — Continuous × continuous {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Salt and age ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_i <- lm(sbp ~ salt * age + bmi + activity + sex + smoker, data = ncd) round(summary(m_i)$coefficients["salt:age", ], 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) 0.0502 0.0052 9.6286 0.0000 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} `salt * age` = `salt + age + salt:age`. The interaction is **+0.050 mmHg per g/day per year of age** (p < 0.001): **the effect of salt grows 0.05 mmHg per g/day for every year of age**. ::: ## Simple slopes ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} b <- coef(m_i) round(sapply(c(30, 45, 60), function(a) b[["salt"]] + a * b[["salt:age"]]), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.01 0.74 1.49 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} emtrends(m_i, ~ age, var = "salt", at = list(age = c(30, 45, 60))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` age salt.trend SE df lower.CL upper.CL 30 -0.0136 0.1000 3992 -0.210 0.183 45 0.7391 0.0727 3992 0.597 0.882 60 1.4917 0.1130 3992 1.270 1.713 Results are averaged over the levels of: sex, smoker Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Age 30**: no effect of salt (−0.01 mmHg per g/day) - **Age 45**: +0.74; **age 60**: +1.49, twice as much - **"The effect of salt"** has **no single value**: it depends on age - `emtrends` gives the slopes with **CIs** at chosen ages ::: ## Plot it ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- expand.grid(salt = seq(3, 18, 1), age = c(30, 45, 60)) |> mutate(bmi = mean(ncd$bmi), activity = mean(ncd$activity), sex = factor("Male", levels = levels(ncd$sex)), smoker = 0) g$fit <- predict(m_i, g) ggplot(g, aes(salt, fit, colour = factor(age))) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_green, col_blue, col_red)) + labs(x = "Salt (g/day)", y = "Predicted SBP (mmHg)", colour = "Age") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s4_interaction_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.key} **Fan-shaped lines**: flat at 30, steeper at 60. An interaction shows as **non-parallel lines**. ::: ## Centring ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ncd <- ncd |> mutate(age45 = age - 45) m_c <- lm(sbp ~ salt * age45 + bmi + activity + sex + smoker, data = ncd) round(c(salt_uncentred = coef(m_i)[["salt"]], salt_centred = coef(m_c)[["salt"]]), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` salt_uncentred salt_centred -1.519 0.739 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} With an interaction, the **"main effect" of salt is the effect when age = 0**: meaningless. **Centre** age (here at 45) and the salt coefficient becomes the effect **at age 45** (0.74). The **interaction** coefficient does **not** change. ::: # Topic 2 — Categorical and scales {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Smoking × sex for CVD risk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g_ss <- glm(cvd10 ~ age + bmi + I(bmi^2) + sex * smoker, data = ncd, family = binomial) round(summary(g_ss)$coefficients["sexMale:smoker", ], 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) 0.824 0.304 2.714 0.007 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} emmeans(g_ss, ~ smoker | sex, type = "response") |> pairs(reverse = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sex = Female: contrast odds.ratio SE df null z.ratio p.value smoker1 / smoker0 0.993 0.260 Inf 1 -0.026 0.9790 sex = Male: contrast odds.ratio SE df null z.ratio p.value smoker1 / smoker0 2.264 0.348 Inf 1 5.321 <0.0001 Tests are performed on the log odds ratio scale ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} Smoking: **OR about 1.0 in women** and **2.3 in men**. The interaction term (log-OR 0.82, **p = 0.007**) tests whether the two odds ratios **differ**. ::: ## Additive scale ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nd <- expand.grid(sex = factor(c("Female", "Male"), levels = levels(ncd$sex)), smoker = c(0, 1), age = 50, bmi = 25) nd$risk <- round(100 * predict(g_ss, nd, type = "response"), 1) nd ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sex smoker age bmi risk 1 Female 0 50 25 4.1 2 Male 0 50 25 5.1 3 Female 1 50 25 4.0 4 Male 1 50 25 10.8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Risk (%) for a 50-year-old with BMI 25: women **4.1 vs 4.0**; men **5.1 vs 10.8** - Risk difference: about **0** in women, **5.7 percentage points** in men - An interaction on the **ratio (multiplicative)** scale and on the **additive** scale can **differ**; public health decisions use the **additive** scale (**absolute risk**) - Always show **predicted risks**, not only odds ratios ::: # Topic 3 — Testing and caution {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## The subgroup p-value trap ::: {.bad} "Smoking is **significant in men** (p < 0.001) but **not in women** (p = 0.98), so sex **modifies** the effect." **This is not a valid test.** A difference in **significance** is not a **significant difference**. Test the **interaction term** (here p = 0.007), and show both **estimates with CIs**. ::: ## Good practice ::: {.good} 1. **Pre-specify** a few plausible interactions (from theory) 2. Test the **interaction term**, then report **stratum-specific estimates** with CIs 3. Interactions need **a lot more data** than main effects (roughly **four times**, for equal-sized groups): do not expect power 4. **Many** interactions tried = **false positives**: report how many you tested 5. Plot **predictions**; centre continuous variables ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 4 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `curves-workshop/labs/lab4_interaction.R` - salt × age: coefficient, simple slopes, `emtrends` - centring and a plot of predictions - smoking × sex: odds ratios within sex, additive scale ::: **Time:** 40 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="k4q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="ynhjd6.6h8bmg" data-show="RWFjaCB5ZWFyIG9mIGFnZSBhZGRzIGFib3V0IDAuMDUgbW1IZyB0byB0aGUgZWZmZWN0IG9m IDEgZy9kYXkgb2Ygc2FsdA==" data-explain="VGhlIHNsb3BlIGZvciBzYWx0IGlzIHRoZSBzYWx0IGNvZWZmaWNpZW50IHBsdXMgMC4wNSB0 aW1lcyBhZ2UsIHNvIHRoZSBlZmZlY3Qgb2Ygc2FsdCBpbmNyZWFzZXMgYnkgMC4wNSBtbUhn IHBlciBnL2RheSBmb3IgZWFjaCB5ZWFyIG9mIGFnZS4="} In the model with salt * age the interaction coefficient is 0.05. What does it mean? - Salt raises SBP by 0.05 mmHg per g/day, whatever the age of each adult - Each year of age adds about 0.05 mmHg to the effect of 1 g/day of salt - Salt and age together explain 5% of the variance in blood pressure - The effect of salt is 0.05 mmHg at the average age of the sample ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="k4q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="ynhwlx.6h8q3v" data-show="SXQgbm93IHNob3dzIHRoZSBlZmZlY3Qgb2Ygc2FsdCBhdCBhZ2UgNDUsIGluc3RlYWQgb2Yg YXQgYWdlIDA=" data-explain="V2l0aCBhbiBpbnRlcmFjdGlvbiwgdGhlIGxvd2VyLW9yZGVyIGNvZWZmaWNpZW50IGlzIHRo ZSBlZmZlY3Qgd2hlbiB0aGUgb3RoZXIgdmFyaWFibGUgaXMgemVyby4gQ2VudHJpbmcgbW92 ZXMgdGhhdCBwb2ludCB0byBhIG1lYW5pbmdmdWwgYWdlLiBUaGUgaW50ZXJhY3Rpb24gY29l ZmZpY2llbnQgaXMgdW5jaGFuZ2VkLg=="} After age is centred at 45, the salt coefficient changes. Why? - The centring changes the interaction coefficient as well as the main one - The centred model fits better, so all the coefficients are re-estimated - Salt is rescaled by the standard deviation of age - It now shows the effect of salt at age 45, instead of at age 0 ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="k4q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="yni9uj.6h94l5" data-show="Tm86IHRlc3QgdGhlIGludGVyYWN0aW9uIHRlcm0sIG5vdCB0aGUgcC12YWx1ZXMgd2l0aGlu IGVhY2ggc2V4" data-explain="QSBkaWZmZXJlbmNlIGluIHNpZ25pZmljYW5jZSBpcyBub3QgYSBzaWduaWZpY2FudCBkaWZm ZXJlbmNlLiBUaGUgaW50ZXJhY3Rpb24gdGVybSB0ZXN0cyBkaXJlY3RseSB3aGV0aGVyIHRo ZSB0d28gb2RkcyByYXRpb3MgZGlmZmVyLg=="} Smoking is clearly harmful in men (OR 2.3) but not in women (OR 1.0). Does this prove effect modification? - No: test the interaction term, not the p-values within each sex - Yes, since the effect is significant in one subgroup and not the other - Yes, because the two odds ratios differ by more than a whole unit - No, because effect modification needs a randomised trial to be shown ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="k4q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="ynin3a.6h9j2k" data-show="QWJvdXQgNS43IHBlcmNlbnRhZ2UgcG9pbnRzIGluIG1lbiBhbmQgY2xvc2UgdG8gemVybyBp biB3b21lbg==" data-explain="VGhlIGFkZGl0aXZlLXNjYWxlIGVmZmVjdCBpcyB0aGUgZGlmZmVyZW5jZSBpbiBwcmVkaWN0 ZWQgcmlza3Mgd2l0aGluIGVhY2ggc2V4OiAxMC44IC0gNS4xID0gNS43IGluIG1lbiwgYW5k IDQuMCAtIDQuMSBhYm91dCAwIGluIHdvbWVuLg=="} Predicted 10-year risk for smokers vs non-smokers: men 10.8% vs 5.1%, women 4.0% vs 4.1%. What are the risk differences for smoking? - About 2.1 percentage points in men and 4.0 percentage points in women - About 2.3 percentage points in men and 1.0 percentage points in women - About 5.7 percentage points in men and close to zero in women - About 10.8 percentage points in men and 4.0 percentage points in women ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="k4q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="ynj0by.6h9xjw" data-show="VGhlIGludGVyYWN0aW9uIGNvbXBhcmVzIHN1Ymdyb3VwIGVmZmVjdHMsIHNvIGl0cyB2YXJp YW5jZSBpcyBsYXJnZXI=" data-explain="VGhlIGludGVyYWN0aW9uIGNvbXBhcmVzIGVzdGltYXRlcyBmcm9tIHN1Ymdyb3VwcywgZWFj aCBiYXNlZCBvbiBwYXJ0IG9mIHRoZSBzYW1wbGUsIHNvIGl0cyBzdGFuZGFyZCBlcnJvciBp cyBsYXJnZXIgdGhhbiB0aGF0IG9mIGEgbWFpbiBlZmZlY3Qu"} Why is a study often underpowered for an interaction even when it has power for the main effect? - Interactions need a continuous variable, which loses information in the study - The interaction compares subgroup effects, so its variance is larger - The main effect uses all the data, while the interaction uses none of it - Software reduces the sample size by the number of product terms in the model ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - `a * b` = `a + b + a:b`; the interaction = **difference in effects** - **Simple slopes** with `emtrends`/`emmeans`; **plot** non-parallel lines - **Centre** so that main effects mean something - Show **absolute risks** (additive scale) as well as ORs - Test the **interaction term**, not subgroup p-values; **pre-specify** ::: **Next:** Session 5: choosing, checking and reporting

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
